label: Psychology
title: Negativity Bias – Why One Bad Moment Outweighs Ten Good Ones
thumbnail_text: Why bad sticks and good slips away
description: Ten compliments and one criticism – and you remember the criticism. This is not a personal flaw. Psychologists call it the negativity bias, and it shows up almost everywhere they look. In this calm video essay we explore the research behind the famous paper 'Bad is stronger than good', what Paul Rozin and Edward Royzman found about negativity dominance, why losses feel heavier than gains, where this bias may come from – and a few simple ways to give the good a fair hearing.

sections.text:
You get ten pieces of feedback on something you made. Nine are warm. One is critical. That evening, lying in bed, which one are you thinking about?

Most of us know the answer without having to think. The nine kind words fade by dinner. The one sharp sentence stays with us for days.

It is tempting to see this as a personal weakness. Too sensitive, too insecure. But when psychologists started to look closely, they found that this pattern is not unusual at all. It seems to be one of the most consistent features of the human mind.

sections.heading: Bad Is Stronger Than Good
sections.text:
In 2001, the psychologist Roy Baumeister and three colleagues published a long review with a blunt title. Bad is stronger than good.

They had gathered research from many different areas of psychology. Close relationships, first impressions, feedback, memory, learning, health, everyday moods. And across these areas, they found the same basic pattern again and again. Bad events tend to have a stronger and longer-lasting effect on us than good events of a similar size.

A harsh word tends to weigh more than a kind one. A bad day can colour the following day, while a good day often leaves fewer traces. A single unpleasant impression of a person can be hard to undo, while a pleasant one can be lost quickly.

The authors were careful to point out that this does not make life mostly bad. Good things usually happen far more often than bad ones. But one by one, the bad tends to carry more weight.

sections.heading: A Drop of Poison
sections.text:
In the same year, the psychologists Paul Rozin and Edward Royzman published their own review, and they gave the pattern a name: the negativity bias.

They described several sides of it. Negative events tend to feel more powerful. They tend to grab our attention faster. And when good and bad are mixed together, the bad often dominates the overall impression.

Rozin, who spent much of his career studying disgust, liked to illustrate this with food. If a cockroach briefly touches a plate of your favourite meal, the whole plate can feel ruined. But there is no equivalent in the other direction. There is no single good ingredient that can make a spoiled dish feel safe again.

The mind seems to treat contamination as contagious, and goodness as fragile. A little bad can spoil a lot of good. A little good rarely redeems a lot of bad.

Research with brain recordings points the same way. In a study published in 1998, Tiffany Ito, John Cacioppo and their colleagues showed people pleasant, unpleasant and neutral pictures. The brain's electrical response tended to be larger for the unpleasant ones, even when people were simply sorting the images.

sections.heading: Why Losses Feel Heavier
sections.text:
Something similar appears in the way we think about money.

In 1979, the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published prospect theory, an influential model of how people make decisions under risk. One of its central ideas is that losses loom larger than gains.

Losing a hundred euros tends to hurt more than finding a hundred euros feels good. In many experiments, people turned down a fair coin toss, win some money or lose some money, unless the possible win was clearly larger than the possible loss. Often it needed to be somewhere around twice as large before people felt comfortable.

Kahneman and Tversky called this loss aversion. Later researchers have debated how strong and how universal it really is. But the basic asymmetry is familiar to almost everyone. We feel what we lose more sharply than what we gain.

sections.heading: A Mind Built for Danger

quote.lead: Two thousand years ago, Seneca noticed a related habit of the mind. In a letter to his friend Lucilius, he wrote:
quote.text: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
quote.author: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 13.4 – transl. R. M. Gummere (1917)

sections.text:
Why would our minds work this way? Researchers usually offer an evolutionary explanation, and it is worth holding it a little loosely, because it is hard to test directly.

The idea goes like this. For our ancestors, missing one opportunity was usually not a disaster. You could find food tomorrow. But missing one threat could be the end. Overlooking a predator or a poisonous plant even once could mean you never got another chance.

A mind that paid a little extra attention to danger, and remembered it a little longer, may have had an advantage. Not a happier mind. A more careful one.

The problem is that this alarm system does not know it lives in a modern world. It reacts to a critical email with some of the same urgency it once reserved for a rustle in the grass.

sections.heading: Giving the Good a Fair Hearing
sections.text:
The negativity bias is not something you can simply switch off. And it would not be wise to try. Paying attention to problems is useful. But you can gently rebalance where your attention goes.

The first step is to name it. When one criticism is spinning in your head, you can tell yourself: this is the negativity bias. The criticism may still be worth taking seriously. But its weight in your mind is not the same as its weight in reality.

The second step is to linger. Good moments often pass through us quickly. A kind word, a warm cup of tea, a moment of sunlight. When you notice one, stay with it for a few breaths longer than you normally would. Psychologists call this savouring. It does not change what happened. It changes how much of it you actually take in.

The third step is to keep a record. In the evening, write down three things that went well that day, however small. Not to pretend the bad did not happen. Simply to make sure the good gets written down too.

And in relationships, it can help to remember the asymmetry. If one harsh word weighs more than one kind word, then a single apology is often not enough. The good needs to arrive more often than the bad, again and again.

The relationship researcher John Gottman, whose work Baumeister and his colleagues discuss, observed couples talking through their disagreements. In the couples who stayed together, positive moments clearly outnumbered negative ones, by roughly five to one. Not zero conflict. Simply much more warmth around it.

sections.heading: Seeing the Whole Picture
sections.text:
Go back to those ten pieces of feedback. Nine kind, one critical. The critical one is real, and it may even be useful. But it is one tenth of the truth, not all of it.

Your mind will probably keep giving the bad a louder voice. That is how it was built. But you do not have to let it have the last word. You can notice the alarm, thank it for trying to protect you, and still choose to look at the rest of the picture.

The bad shouts. The good tends to whisper. Sometimes, all it needs is someone who is willing to listen.

short.hook: Why one criticism beats nine compliments
short.title: Why bad sticks and good slips away
short.text:
Nine compliments. One criticism. Which one are you thinking about tonight?

In 2001, psychologists reviewed research from relationships, feedback, memory and learning. Their conclusion was the title of the paper. Bad is stronger than good.

A cockroach can ruin a whole plate of food. But no single ingredient can make a spoiled dish safe again.

For our ancestors, missing one opportunity was rarely a disaster. Missing one threat could be the end.

So the bad shouts, and the good whispers. Tonight, write down three things that went well. Not to deny the bad. Just to let the good be heard.
